name: Cross-Race Effect
description: People are usually better at recognizing and telling apart faces from their own racial group than faces from another group. The effect is not just a verbal belief that “they all look alike” — it shows up in actual memory and discrimination performance.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to biometrics, identity verification, moderation review, photo/avatar-heavy products, eyewitness-style workflows, and synthetic-data evaluation. Both humans and systems can under-distinguish out-group faces if the design or training setup is careless.
prevalence_note: Well known in eyewitness-memory, face-perception, and fairness/biometrics conversations, and occasionally relevant to trust-and-safety or identity products, but not a routine named heuristic in general UX practice.

findings.description: Updating two decades of research, this meta-analysis treats the cross-race recognition deficit as a robust pattern: people recognize same-race faces more accurately than cross-race faces. It also finds that greater cross-race contact is associated with a smaller deficit (r = -0.15), with stronger moderation when contact occurs in childhood or is experimentally manipulated.
findings.effect_size: r = -0.15 (cross-race contact associated with smaller recognition deficit)
findings.source_title: Does Cross-Race Contact Improve Cross-Race Face Perception? A Meta-Analysis of the Cross-Race Deficit and Contact
